newsitem.title: USA: Spec for new CBOT wheat contract due by fall-Arbor.
newsitem.headline: Spec for new CBOT wheat contract due by fall-Arbor.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade chairman Patrick Arbor said he expected specifications for a planned new wheat contract, possibly to share with the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange, to be available in six to nine months.
"We have a committee at the Board of Trade looking into the possibility of developing an international wheat contract," Arbor told Reuters at a Risk Management Conference here.
"I would imagine our committee should have something out in six to nine months," Arbor said.
"If we develop that contract, naturally we'll share it with LIFFE," Arbor said.

He said the wheat contract had lower priority now at CBOT than other issues, such as linkage of open-outcry trading with LIFFE in government bonds in May and startup of the Chicago Bond Brokerage electronic cash bond trading system by September.
"I would say this is on a back burner right now," he said.
Arbor said the wheat contract's shape remains vague.
"It could be soft or hard wheat but obviously it should at least be of milling quality and should be able to meet international standards," Arbor said.
"If it's going to be physically deliverable, it should have international delivery points. It could be an index (of various wheats)," Arbor said.

LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth, who was present at the Arbor interview, said a wheat linkage with CBOT was important but a less urgent issue for LIFFE because the exchange has directed its resources toward competition with European exchanges ahead of the planned European Monetary Union in 1999.
"It doesn't have the priority the EMU developments do," he said, but he added that LIFFE was actively researching other contracts to introduce in view of dramatic changes in Europe.

The prospects for agricultural derivatives look promising as European farmers and end-users grow more aware of the need for hedging, he said. Wigglesworth said prices of agricultural products in Europe were increasingly determined by market forces.
